pl-l4d11c2-d1e115.summary: Answers the question how this can happen briefly: the mystery of faith can be believed with profit but not investigated with profit.
claims: The mystery of faith is to be believed, not investigated.

pl-l4d11c2-d1e121.summary: Attributes the fact that Christ's body is not increased by the bread's change, nor his blood by the wine's, to the will and power of him who brought the same body from the Virgin: that substance becomes this without its increase.
claims: Christ's body is not increased by the conversion, by divine power.

pl-l4d11c2-d1e124.summary: Reports that some do not grant that the substance of bread is ever Christ's flesh, though it becomes it, as flour became bread and water became wine, though we do not say flour is bread or water is wine.
claims: Some deny that bread is ever Christ's flesh, though it becomes it.

pl-l4d11c2-d1e128.summary: Reports that others grant that what was bread or wine is, after consecration, the body and blood, but deny that 'bread is Christ's flesh' follows, since the substance of bread, once made Christ's flesh, is no longer the substance of bread but flesh.
claims: What was bread is Christ's body, but bread is not Christ's body.

pl-l4d11c2-d1e131.summary: Distinguishes: 'the substance of bread, or what was bread, is now Christ's body' is true not of bread remaining, which is not Christ's body, but of it as changed, what it has become. Nor is the substance of bread the matter of the body, since the body is not formed from it as from matter; it is changed into it.
claims: The substance of bread as changed is Christ's body.
The bread is not matter of Christ's body but is changed into it.

pl-l4d11c2-d1e134.summary: Quotes Augustine's De Trinitate: we call Christ's body what is taken from the fruits of the earth and consecrated by mystic prayer, received in memory of the Lord's passion; brought to that visible form by human hands, it is sanctified to be so great a sacrament only by the Spirit of God working invisibly.
claims: The sacrament is sanctified by the Spirit working invisibly.

pl-l4d11c2-d1e143.summary: Reports a view that the conversion means that under the accidents under which the substance of bread and wine was, after consecration the substance of the body and blood is, without being affected by them; bread is said to pass into the body because where bread was, Christ's body now is.
claims: Some hold that Christ's body comes to be under the accidents where bread was.

pl-l4d11c2-d1e146.summary: Asks what then becomes of the substance of bread and wine, and reports their answer: it is resolved into prior matter or reduced to nothing.
claims: Some hold that the bread is resolved into matter or annihilated.

pl-l4d11c2-d1e149.summary: Reports others who thought the substance of bread and wine remains there together with Christ's body and blood, and that one substance becomes the other because where one is the other is too, and who call the substance of bread and wine the sacrament.
claims: Some hold that the substance of bread remains with Christ's body.

pl-l4d11c2-d1e153.summary: Rejects this: that no substance is there but Christ's body and blood is shown by what has been said and what follows.
claims: Only Christ's body and blood are present as substance.

pl-l4d11c2-d1e156.summary: Quotes Ambrose: the bread we receive in the mystery is the bread formed by the Spirit's hand in the Virgin's womb and baked by the fire of the passion on the altar of the cross; the living bread and the flesh given for the world are not two but one bread and one flesh, one body, that taken from the Virgin, which rose and ascended.
claims: The eucharistic bread is the one body born of the Virgin.

pl-l4d11c2-d1e165.summary: Quotes Gregory: no believer can doubt that at the hour of the sacrifice the heavens open at the priest's voice, choirs of angels are present, the highest and lowest are joined, and one thing is made of visible and invisible.
claims: The eucharist joins heaven and earth.

pl-l4d11c2-d1e174.summary: Adds Gregory: at the same moment it is taken to heaven to be joined to Christ's body by the angels' ministry and seen on the altar; as the Word's divinity fills the world, that body is consecrated in many places, yet there are not many bodies of Christ but one; whether one receives more or less, all receive Christ's body wholly and equally.
claims: Christ's body consecrated in many places is one body.
All receive the whole body equally.

pl-l4d11c2-d1e180.summary: Concludes that after consecration there is no substance of bread or wine, though the species remain, the appearance of bread and wine and their taste; so one thing is seen and another understood.
claims: After consecration no substance of bread or wine remains.
The species and taste remain.

pl-l4d11c2.summary: Asked how the conversion can happen, Lombard answers that the mystery of faith can be believed but not investigated with profit; that Christ's body is not increased is due to the will and power of him who brought it from the Virgin. Some deny that the substance of bread ever is Christ's flesh, though it becomes it; others grant that what was bread is the body, but not that bread is the body; Lombard distinguishes: the substance of bread, as changed, is Christ's body, and it is not matter of the body but is changed into it. He reports two further views, that the substance of bread is annihilated or resolved into matter while the body is under the accidents, and that the substance of bread remains with the body, and rejects the latter: Ambrose and Gregory show that only Christ's body and blood are there. After consecration, no substance of bread or wine remains, though their species and taste do.
claims: The mystery of the conversion is to be believed, not investigated.
The substance of bread is changed into, not used as matter of, Christ's body.
Some hold that the bread is annihilated or resolved into matter.
The view that the substance of bread remains with Christ's body is rejected.
After consecration only the species of bread and wine remain, not their substance.
